tagline: Own the outcome. Know your limits.
overview: Accountability as a professional concept — standards, the five components, socialization, and the factors that shape practice — plus Exemplar 42.A Competence, taught from your Unit 7 slides and study guide.

topics.title: Accountability Foundations: Top-of-License Practice, Autonomy, Governance & the Five Components
Accountability at the Bedside: Expanded Duties, Related Concepts, Delegation & Unsafe Orders
Exemplar 42.A Competence: Critical Thinking, Emotional Intelligence, Benner’s Stages & Practicing Within Your Limits

flashcards.front: Define accountability
flashcards.back: Being answerable for your own nursing judgments, actions, and omissions and their outcomes—to the client, profession, employer, and law. It cannot be transferred.

flashcards.front: Accountability vs responsibility?
flashcards.back: Responsibility = the duty to do a task (can be assigned/delegated). Accountability = answering for the judgment and outcome (stays with the professional).

flashcards.front: Define Top-of-License (TOL) practice
flashcards.back: An interprofessional approach that lets nurses practice to the fullest extent of their education, knowledge, skills, and legal scope (IOM 2010, The Future of Nursing), focused on outcomes and safe transitions, including advocating for nurses’ autonomy.

flashcards.front: Professional vs individual autonomy
flashcards.back: Professional: nursing self-regulates, sets standards, writes policy, and defines scope through boards of nursing. Individual: the nurse’s freedom and accountability to act within scope and advocate for safe, evidence-based care.

flashcards.front: Define governance
flashcards.back: The organizational structure, provided by professional nursing organizations, that establishes social, political, and economic arrangements giving nurses control over their practice, self-discipline, and working conditions.

flashcards.front: Name the five components that promote professional accountability
flashcards.back: Education • Body of knowledge • Service orientation • Allegiance to a code of ethics • Autonomy and membership in a professional organization (E-B-S-C-A).

flashcards.front: A nurse volunteers with the Medical Reserve Corps during a pandemic. Which component?
flashcards.back: Service orientation—service to others ahead of profit.

flashcards.front: What legally defines whether a task is within the RN’s scope?
flashcards.back: The Nurse Practice Act and board of nursing rules of the state where the client is located. Facility policy can restrict but never expand scope.

flashcards.front: You discover your own medication error and the client seems fine. What do you do?
flashcards.back: Assess the client, notify the provider, document the facts truthfully, and complete an event report. ‘No harm’ is not a reason to stay silent.

flashcards.front: A colleague asks you to co-sign a waste you didn’t witness. Response?
flashcards.back: Decline—signing would falsify the record and enable diversion—and notify the charge nurse per controlled-substance policy.

flashcards.front: Best way to change a unit routine that conflicts with current evidence?
flashcards.back: Bring the evidence to the practice council, educator, or EBP committee (shared governance)—not quiet noncompliance or blind continuation.

flashcards.front: Course vs current: Magnet hospitals and the BSN
flashcards.back: Course guide: Magnet hospitals require BSN-prepared nurses. Current standard: Magnet requires a BSN or higher for nurse managers and leaders, plus a plan to grow BSN staff. Expect the course wording on course exams.

flashcards.front: Course vs current: who regulates the nursing code of ethics?
flashcards.back: Course guide: codes are “regulated alongside state boards via the NCSBN.” Current standard: the ANA writes the Code of Ethics for Nurses; boards enforce the Nurse Practice Act. NCLEX: the Code belongs to the ANA.

flashcards.front: List the expanded duties of accountability
flashcards.back: Holistic health & wellness • Physical outcomes • Safety • Trauma, abuse & self-directed violence • Client and self-education • Infection prevention & immunity.

flashcards.front: Comfort accountability: what are the three nursing implications?
flashcards.back: Assess comfort at least once per shift (more often as the condition requires) • Report deviations or changes • Document comfort level and all interventions.

flashcards.front: Client says “I’m fine” but is grimacing, trembling, and hypertensive. Next step?
flashcards.back: Complete the assessment before leaving the room—explore and rate the pain; words and cues conflict.

flashcards.front: Client refuses opioids out of fear. Accountable response?
flashcards.back: Respect the choice but explore the fear, educate, offer non-opioid and nonpharmacologic options, notify the provider, and reassess—don’t just document the refusal.

flashcards.front: Five rights of delegation
flashcards.back: Right task • Right circumstance • Right person • Right directions/communication • Right supervision/evaluation.

flashcards.front: What can the RN never delegate to UAP?
flashcards.back: Assessment, care planning/nursing judgment, initial teaching, evaluation, and care of unstable or unpredictable clients (remember EAT: Evaluate, Assess, Teach).

flashcards.front: An LPN discards urine that was supposed to be strained. Is the RN accountable?
flashcards.back: Yes. The LPN answers for performing the task; the RN retains accountability for the assignment, clear directions, supervision, and outcome.

flashcards.front: A prescriber refuses to change an order you believe is unsafe. What now?
flashcards.back: Do not carry it out; tell the prescriber you’re holding it; escalate through the chain of command (charge nurse → supervisor → medical director/CNO); keep monitoring; document facts.

flashcards.front: Is a nurse accountable when a correctly given PRN opioid fails to relieve pain?
flashcards.back: Not for the drug’s pharmacologic failure—but yes for assessing, dosing within the order, reassessing, and notifying the provider if relief is inadequate.

flashcards.front: Suspected child abuse: do you need proof before reporting?
flashcards.back: No. Report reasonable suspicion to the designated agency (in NC, county DSS), document objectively, and protect the child; do not investigate or confront.

flashcards.front: Just Culture responses
flashcards.back: Human error → console and fix the system • At-risk behavior → coach • Reckless behavior → sanction/discipline.

flashcards.front: Should you document “incident report filed” in the chart?
flashcards.back: No. The event report is a confidential QI document; chart only the factual care and the client’s condition.

flashcards.front: Name the seven related concepts in the accountability matrix (p. 2705)
flashcards.back: Comfort • Evidence-based practice • Health, wellness, illness & injury • Infection • Safety • Teaching & learning • Trauma.

flashcards.front: Trauma: the three nursing implications in the matrix
flashcards.back: Assess for physical, emotional, or sexual abuse • Screen for abuse risk AND suicide risk on admission • Stay alert for spoken or shown warning signs of abuse or suicide.

flashcards.front: Teaching & learning: nursing implications in the matrix
flashcards.back: Assess client and family learning needs and readiness • Design teaching from EBP • Read current journals and attend workshops/seminars • Keep competence through continuing education. Also guide preceptees and students.

flashcards.front: Ms. Miller refuses opioids. With whom should the nurse and charge nurse collaborate?
flashcards.back: The primary HCP or hospitalist • The clinical pharmacist (non-narcotic or multimodal options safe with her GI diagnosis) • Possibly a pain management specialist or a physical/integrative therapist.

flashcards.front: Define competence
flashcards.back: Practicing to the fullest extent with specialized knowledge, skills, abilities, and clinical judgment—applying critical thinking, problem solving, and ethical reasoning, with awareness of one’s limits and openness to feedback.

flashcards.front: Define emotional intelligence (EI)
flashcards.back: A nurse’s ability to recognize, through emotional appraisal, when personal emotions rather than objective knowledge are influencing clinical decisions.

flashcards.front: Three core areas of competence
flashcards.back: Critical thinking • Problem solving (supported by EI) • Ethical reasoning and decision making.

flashcards.front: Benner’s five stages in order
flashcards.back: Novice → Advanced beginner → Competent (≈2–3 yrs) → Proficient (≈3–5 yrs) → Expert.

flashcards.front: Novice vs advanced beginner
flashcards.back: Novice (student): context-free rules, inflexible. Advanced beginner (new grad): marginally acceptable; recognizes recurring meaningful aspects from some experience.

flashcards.front: A nurse sees situations as wholes, uses maxims, and plans long-term goals. Which stage?
flashcards.back: Proficient (≈3–5 years).

flashcards.front: What is the first rule of competence?
flashcards.back: Always ask for help whenever there is any uncertainty about the safety of an action. “I don’t know—would you help me?” beats guessing.

flashcards.front: Do expert nurses still double-check high-alert medications?
flashcards.back: Yes. Expert vigilance means continuing to double-check high-risk actions such as doses and sterilization.

flashcards.front: You’re floated to a unit where you lack competence. What do you do?
flashcards.back: Before taking report, tell the supervisor the specific gap, decline an independent assignment you can’t do safely, and negotiate a safe role (supportive tasks, buddy, or a unit where you’re competent).

flashcards.front: Four core elements of cultural competence training
flashcards.back: Recognize your own values/beliefs • Develop listening skills and learn cultural rites/traditions • Advocate when treatment conflicts with cultural values • Identify community resources for follow-up.

flashcards.front: A family member offers to interpret consent information. Accept?
flashcards.back: No. Use a qualified medical interpreter; family members (especially minors) may misinterpret or filter information.

flashcards.front: Exhausted after 20 hours awake and asked to stay. Competent response?
flashcards.back: Decline the extra shift because you can’t practice safely, and help find coverage; fitness for duty is part of competence.

flashcards.front: Exemplar 42.A learning outcomes
flashcards.back: 1. Analyze competence as it relates to accountability. 2. Describe the areas of competence. 3. Explain the importance of lifelong competence for nurses.

flashcards.front: Define situational learning
flashcards.back: Applying classroom theory to diverse, real-world clinical situations. It is how critical thinking deepens at the bedside after nursing school.

flashcards.front: How does competence grow across a career (course list)?
flashcards.back: Formal education • Seminars • Peer-reviewed journals • Employer classes • Interprofessional collaboration. To close a gap: continuing education, workshops, literature, mentorship/preceptorship, supervised orientation.

flashcards.front: Accountability and responsibility: slide definitions
flashcards.back: Accountability = being answerable for the outcomes of a task or assignment. Responsibility = the specific obligation tied to the duties of a particular role.

flashcards.front: Can a nurse be accountable for someone else’s actions?
flashcards.back: Yes. Nurses answer for their own actions and may also be accountable for subordinates or trainees they supervise, such as students, orientees, or staff they delegate to.

flashcards.front: Define standards of practice (standards of care)
flashcards.back: Professional standards or guidelines that say what a nurse should and should not do. Established by organizations such as The Joint Commission, ANA, and NLN; they describe the responsibilities nurses are accountable for.

flashcards.front: National guidance on accountability comes in what three forms?
flashcards.back: Benchmarks of patient care, standards of nursing practice, and codes of ethics.

flashcards.front: The Joint Commission vs ANA Standards of Nursing Practice
flashcards.back: TJC: standards focus on healthcare organizations (accreditation). ANA: describes responsibilities US nurses are accountable for; follows the nursing process plus Standards of Professional Performance.

flashcards.front: ANA Standards of Practice follow which steps?
flashcards.back: The nursing process: assessment, diagnosis, outcomes identification, planning, implementation, and evaluation. Standards of Professional Performance cover behaviors such as ethics, communication, collaboration, leadership, education, and quality.

flashcards.front: National League for Nursing (NLN)
flashcards.back: A national nursing organization the course lists as a source of standards; its focus is nursing education and nurse educators.

flashcards.front: What is a Nurse Practice Act?
flashcards.back: The law each state passes to regulate nursing practice and define legal scope. In NC: the Nursing Practice Act, G.S. 90-171.19 et seq., enforced by the NCBON.

flashcards.front: Codes of ethics: three slide points
flashcards.back: 1) Respect the inherent worth and dignity of all people. 2) Do what is right, even at personal cost. 3) Codes change as society’s needs and values change.

flashcards.front: Why acknowledge successes as well as errors?
flashcards.back: Owning both keeps the professional culture positive. Honoring successes is as important as examining and correcting errors.

flashcards.front: What is QSEN?
flashcards.back: Quality and Safety Education for Nurses: a national initiative to improve quality and safety in nursing.

flashcards.front: Why does accountability need clear standards?
flashcards.back: You can only answer for a role that is clearly defined. Clear standards of care let a nurse’s performance be measured, and accountability shapes the response to errors and incident reporting.

flashcards.front: Components of accountability: the slide list (slide 7)
flashcards.back: 1) Completing a program that gives the body of knowledge for the role. 2) A focus toward service. 3) Allegiance to a code of ethics. 4) Autonomy of the role. 5) Membership in a professional organization.

flashcards.front: Autonomy (slide 9): what does professional status depend on?
flashcards.back: The profession’s ability to function autonomously: formulate nursing policy, control its own activity, regulate itself, and hold legal authority to define its scope. For the individual: independence, responsibility, and accountability for one’s actions.

flashcards.front: Define socialization
flashcards.back: The process of learning to become a member of a group or society and learning the social rules that define relationships—how to behave, feel, and see the world as others in that role do.

flashcards.front: Why is professional socialization more complex?
flashcards.back: It also requires understanding cultures that promote high performance and safe practice. A high-performance culture is dynamic and ever-changing.

flashcards.front: Four components of a dynamic learning culture
flashcards.back: Transparency • Avoidance of blame • Use of best-practice guidelines • Staff input.

flashcards.front: Components of successful socialization (slide 12)
flashcards.back: Clear expectations, follow-through, rewards/consequences • Interaction with fellow students (a powerful driver) • Clear expectations for preparation and performance • Understanding mistakes and consequences through reflective practice • Focus on student strengths.

flashcards.front: Define reflective practice
flashcards.back: Looking back on an experience, including a mistake, to understand what happened and its consequences and what to do differently.

flashcards.front: What does the NSNA code address?
flashcards.back: The National Student Nurses Association code addresses students’ responsibilities in the academic environment and in society at large.

flashcards.front: Six factors influencing nursing practice and accountability
flashcards.back: Economics • Consumer demand • Science and technology • Information availability and telecommunications • Legislation • Nursing workforce capacity.

flashcards.front: Economics: how has it changed nursing?
flashcards.back: Insurance changes altered demand for nursing care; care is shifting from inpatient to outpatient; acute care remains the primary practice area; more nurses work in community settings; specialties grew; integrated care models aim to control costs.

flashcards.front: Consumer demand: key points
flashcards.back: Consumers = the general public, and their needs drive any service. Demand for integrative health reflects cost control plus interest in complementary approaches. Consumers are more knowledgeable and vocal, partly due to the internet.

flashcards.front: Science and technology: effect on nursing
flashcards.back: Advances affect practice, competence, and accountability. Genetic testing is available outside traditional healthcare. Nurses must expand knowledge and technical skills, use computerized equipment and the EHR, and protect shared data ethically.

flashcards.front: Telehealth vs telenursing vs mHealth
flashcards.back: Telehealth: long-distance healthcare through technology. Telenursing: delivering nursing care through telecommunication. mHealth: mobile health—care through mobile devices. All raise HIPAA privacy and security questions.

flashcards.front: Course vs current: “Electronic Health Report Systems”
flashcards.back: Your slides say “Electronic Health Report Systems.” Current term: electronic health record (EHR). Course exam: recognize the slide wording; NCLEX: EHR.

flashcards.front: Information availability: nurse’s duty
flashcards.back: Clients are better informed through the internet, so nurses must know accurate, reliable websites (e.g., MedlinePlus) and help clients judge sources.

flashcards.front: Patient Self-Determination Act (PSDA)
flashcards.back: Federal law (1990): at admission, adults must be informed in writing of their right to accept or refuse care and to make advance directives. Nurses often ensure compliance. Care never depends on having a directive.

flashcards.front: Course vs current: PSDA “competent adults”
flashcards.back: Slides: all competent adults are informed at admission. Current: Medicare/Medicaid facilities inform every adult; if incapacitated, family or surrogate first, then the client once able. Never require a directive.

flashcards.front: Factors driving the nursing shortage
flashcards.back: Shortage of nursing faculty • Current nurses reaching retirement • Changing demographics • Aging population • High turnover rates.

flashcards.front: Course recommendations for the nursing shortage
flashcards.back: Help students enter and progress through programs faster • Recruit young people early (middle and high school) • Scheduling flexibility, rewards for mentors, adequate staffing, higher salaries • More funding for nursing education. Requires collaboration of health systems, policy makers, educators, and professional organizations.

flashcards.front: Competence: slide definition and how it changed
flashcards.back: Possessing the knowledge and skills to perform one’s job appropriately and safely. Formerly, nurses were competent if they could simply provide care and comfort; today the standard is higher.

flashcards.front: Critical thinkers (slide 4)
flashcards.back: Open to others’ opinions but rely on knowledge as the scientific basis for action; willing to think, inquire, and investigate before deciding. Situational learning = analyze, synthesize, and apply learning.

flashcards.front: Ethical reasoning is based on what?
flashcards.back: The goals, values, and obligations of professional nurses. It is needed in everyday practice, mindful of client preferences, the nurse’s own well-being, personal limits, emotions, and the practice environment.

flashcards.front: Is a nurse accountable when a decision was made with colleagues?
flashcards.back: Yes. Nurses may collaborate with peers and the team on how to respond, but each nurse is accountable for her own choices.

flashcards.front: Benner’s model: core premise
flashcards.back: Experience is essential for developing professional expertise; nurses move through five levels of proficiency: novice, advanced beginner, competent, proficient, expert.

flashcards.front: Concepts related to accountability (slide 10)
flashcards.back: Comfort • Evidence-based practice • Health, wellness, illness, and injury • Infection • Safety • Teaching and learning • Trauma.

flashcards.front: Concept learning outcomes 42.1–42.4
flashcards.back: 42.1 How nursing promotes accountability • 42.2 Accountability and related concepts • 42.3 Socialization to nursing • 42.4 Factors influencing practice and accountability.

questions.stem: While reviewing the medication administration record, a nurse realizes she gave a client furosemide 40 mg orally 1 hour after the provider discontinued it. The client is alert, and vital signs are stable. Which action by the nurse best demonstrates professional accountability?
options: Assess the client, notify the provider, and complete an event report.
Monitor urine output closely and tell no one, since no harm occurred.
Ask the pharmacist to remove the discontinued order from the profile.
Document the dose as held so the record matches the current order.
optionRationales: Correct. Accountability means owning the error: assess for effects (fluid and potassium status), disclose to the provider, document truthfully, and report through the safety system.
Incorrect. Absence of visible harm does not remove the duty to disclose; the provider may need to order labs or adjust care, and unreported errors cannot be learned from.
Incorrect. The order is already discontinued; this does nothing about the dose already given or the duty to disclose.
Incorrect. Charting a dose as held when it was given is falsification of the medical record.
questions.rationale: Accountability covers errors and omissions, not just successes. The accountable sequence is assess the client, communicate with the provider, document the facts truthfully, and file an event report so the system can learn. Monitoring silently is the most tempting distractor because the nurse is doing something clinically useful, but it withholds information the provider needs (for example, to check electrolytes) and hides the event from quality review.
questions.takeaway: When you make an error, assess the client, tell the provider, document truthfully, and report it—no harm is not a reason to stay silent.
questions.hintContent: A discontinued diuretic was given; think about what the provider and the safety system need to know.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate any option that hides, alters, or minimizes information—those are never the accountable choice.

questions.stem: A hospital redesigns staffing on a medical unit so that RNs spend much of each shift transporting stable clients and restocking supplies, and discharge teaching is reduced to printed handouts. Several clients have been readmitted for medication errors at home. A staff RN wants to advocate for top-of-license practice. Which action by the RN is most appropriate?
options: Stop doing the transport and restocking tasks until the staffing plan is changed.
Accept the redesign, since staffing decisions belong only to hospital administration.
Bring the readmission data to the practice council and propose reassigning nonnursing tasks.
Show RN value by doing procedures she has observed but has not been validated to perform.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Refusing assigned work on her own disrupts care and bypasses governance; the accountable route is to advocate through legitimate channels while the plan remains in effect.
Incorrect. Top-of-license practice includes a duty to advocate for nurses’ autonomy, and shared governance gives staff nurses a voice in how nursing work is organized.
Correct. Using outcome data and shared governance to protect RN time for teaching and safe transitions is the accountable way to advocate for top-of-license practice.
Incorrect. Top-of-license practice is bounded by legal scope and validated competence; performing unvalidated procedures is practicing beyond, not at, the top of license.
questions.rationale: Top-of-license practice means each team member works at the full extent of their education, competence, and legal scope, and it requires nurses to be accountable in practice and to advocate for their own and colleagues’ autonomy. Here, RN time is consumed by tasks support staff can do while RN-only work (teaching and safe transitions) is being cut, and the readmissions show the harm. The accountable response is to bring data through shared governance and propose moving nonnursing tasks to other staff. Refusing the tasks is tempting because it seems to defend RN practice, but it is unilateral; accepting the plan silently abandons the advocacy duty; and doing unvalidated procedures exceeds competence.
questions.takeaway: Advocate for top-of-license practice with outcome data through shared governance; never by refusing work unilaterally or by exceeding your competence.
questions.hintContent: Top-of-license practice has two limits—legal scope and personal competence—and includes an advocacy duty.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that act unilaterally, stay silent, or go beyond competence; choose the one that uses data and a legitimate channel.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse educator is teaching newly hired graduates about professional autonomy. Which statement by a new graduate indicates a need for further teaching?
options: “The board of nursing has legal authority to define our scope of practice.”
“If I hold a dose for a safety concern, I must be able to explain my reasoning.”
“Nurses help set the practice standards that other nurses are measured against.”
“Autonomy means I can follow my own methods when they differ from policy.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. This is accurate: professional autonomy includes legal authority vested in state boards of nursing to define scope.
Incorrect. This is accurate: individual autonomy is paired with accountability for one’s judgments.
Incorrect. This is accurate: a self-regulating profession sets standards of practice for its members.
Correct. This statement needs correction: autonomy is freedom to practice within scope, standards, and policy; disagreement with a policy is addressed through governance, not personal workarounds.
questions.rationale: Professional autonomy means nursing self-regulates, sets standards, and holds legal authority through boards of nursing; individual autonomy means the nurse makes and answers for clinical judgments within scope. Autonomy is never permission to ignore policy or standards. A nurse who believes a policy is outdated brings evidence to the practice council or educator. The statement about holding a dose may look like a red flag, but it is a correct example of autonomy exercised accountably.
questions.takeaway: Autonomy is freedom to practice within scope and standards—not freedom from them.
questions.hintContent: Autonomy and accountability are a package; look for the statement that separates them.
questions.hintStrategy: In ‘needs further teaching’ items, find the one statement that is false; treat each option as true/false.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A client who received an IV opioid 45 minutes ago is difficult to arouse and has a respiratory rate of 9 breaths/min. The client’s next scheduled oral opioid dose is now due. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Notify the provider and request a change in the opioid orders.
Withhold the dose, stimulate the client, and assess breathing.
Give the scheduled dose and recheck respirations in 30 minutes.
Complete an event report describing the opioid-related sedation.
optionRationales: Incorrect. The provider must be notified, but the client’s airway and breathing need immediate attention first.
Correct. Holding the dose is an independent nursing judgment, and stimulating the client while assessing airway, breathing, and oxygenation addresses the immediate threat.
Incorrect. Giving more opioid to an oversedated client with respiratory depression could be fatal.
Incorrect. Documentation and reporting come after the client is safe.
questions.rationale: Individual autonomy lets the nurse withhold a medication when the client’s condition makes it unsafe, and accountability requires acting on the immediate threat first. Oversedation with a respiratory rate of 9 is a breathing problem, so the nurse stimulates the client, supports the airway, checks oxygenation, and follows the reversal protocol as indicated before calling the provider. Notifying the provider is the strongest distractor because it is necessary, but it is not the first action while the client is hypoventilating.
questions.takeaway: Hold an opioid for oversedation or respiratory depression and address airway and breathing before calling or documenting.
questions.hintContent: Use ABCs: what is the most immediate physiologic threat?
questions.hintStrategy: When several options are correct actions, choose the one that addresses the immediate physical threat first; notifying and documenting usually follow.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies

questions.stem: A preceptor is describing nursing behaviors that reflect the components promoting professional accountability. Which examples correctly pair a behavior with its component? Select all that apply.
options: Enrolling in an RN-to-BSN program — education
Volunteering with the Medical Reserve Corps during a pandemic — service orientation
Reporting one’s own medication error despite possible criticism — allegiance to a code of ethics
Picking up extra paid overtime to increase income — service orientation
Following a unit routine because senior staff have always done it — body of knowledge
Serving on a professional association’s standards committee — autonomy and professional organization
optionRationales: Correct. Advancing formal nursing education reflects the education component.
Correct. Volunteering to support public health during a crisis is the course’s example of service orientation.
Correct. Doing what is right even at personal cost to maintain moral integrity reflects allegiance to the code of ethics.
Incorrect. Working for extra income is not service orientation, which places service to others ahead of profit.
Incorrect. The body of knowledge is applied through current evidence (EBP), not habit or tradition.
Correct. Participating in a professional organization’s governance reflects autonomy and membership in a professional organization.
questions.rationale: The five components are education, body of knowledge, service orientation, allegiance to a code of ethics, and autonomy with membership in a professional organization. Each is recognized by behavior: advancing education, using evidence, serving others ahead of profit, doing right at personal cost, and participating in professional governance. Following a routine ‘because we always have’ is the opposite of applying a continuously expanding, evidence-based body of knowledge, and paid overtime is employment, not service orientation.
questions.takeaway: Recognize the five components by what nurses do: learn, use evidence, serve, act ethically at personal cost, and take part in professional governance.
questions.hintContent: For each pair, ask whether the behavior truly expresses that component’s purpose.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate SATA options one at a time as true/false; do not look for a set number of answers.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: An RN who recently relocated tells a colleague, “At my old hospital, RNs could remove chest tubes without any order.” Which source should the colleague explain determines whether an action is legally within the RN’s scope of practice?
options: The Nurse Practice Act and board rules where the client is located
The policies of the hospital where the RN was first employed and oriented
The ANA Code of Ethics for Nurses and its interpretive statements
The preferences of the provider who is supervising the client’s care
optionRationales: Correct. Legal scope is defined by state law (the Nurse Practice Act) and board of nursing rules where the client receives care.
Incorrect. A former employer’s policy cannot expand legal scope, and policies apply only within that facility.
Incorrect. The Code of Ethics guides ethical conduct but does not set legal scope of practice.
Incorrect. A provider cannot authorize a nurse to practice beyond the legal scope defined by the state.
questions.rationale: Professional autonomy is exercised through state boards of nursing, which hold legal authority under each state’s Nurse Practice Act to define nursing scope. Facility policy may be stricter than the law but can never expand it, and it changes from employer to employer. The Code of Ethics is a tempting distractor because it is an authoritative professional document, but it governs ethical obligations rather than the legal boundaries of practice.
questions.takeaway: Legal scope comes from the Nurse Practice Act and board rules where the client is located; policies and provider preferences cannot expand it.
questions.hintContent: Distinguish legal scope from ethical guidance and from employer policy.
questions.hintStrategy: When asked what ‘legally’ governs practice, choose the statute or regulatory body over policies, preferences, or ethical codes.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: Near the end of a shift, a colleague asks a nurse to co-sign a hydromorphone waste in the automated dispensing cabinet, saying, “I wasted it an hour ago while you were busy.” Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Co-sign the waste because the colleague is a trusted, experienced nurse.
Co-sign the waste, then report the late documentation to the manager.
Decline to co-sign the unwitnessed waste and notify the charge nurse.
Suggest the colleague describe the waste in a narrative note instead.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Trust does not make an unwitnessed co-signature truthful; signing would falsify a controlled-substance record.
Incorrect. Reporting afterward does not undo the falsified co-signature.
Correct. A witness signature attests to what was observed; declining and notifying the charge nurse follows controlled-substance policy and protects against diversion.
Incorrect. A narrative note does not replace the required witnessed waste and leaves an unresolved discrepancy.
questions.rationale: Allegiance to the code of ethics means doing what is right even when it is uncomfortable. A co-signature states that the nurse personally witnessed the waste; signing for something not witnessed is falsification and is a common pathway for drug diversion. The accountable action is to decline and notify the charge nurse so the discrepancy is resolved under policy. Co-signing and then reporting is tempting because it seems to cover both loyalty and safety, but the nurse would still have falsified a record.
questions.takeaway: Never co-sign a controlled-substance waste you did not witness; decline and escalate the discrepancy per policy.
questions.hintContent: What does a witness signature legally claim?
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options in which the nurse documents something untrue, even if a ‘fix’ is added afterward.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A staff nurse finds several recent systematic reviews indicating that a routine practice on her unit is no longer recommended. The unit policy still requires the routine. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Change her own practice now and teach coworkers to do the same.
Continue the routine without comment because it reflects unit policy.
Ask a provider to write orders that override the policy for her clients.
Bring the evidence to the unit practice council for policy review.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Unilaterally abandoning policy bypasses governance and creates inconsistent care on the unit.
Incorrect. Silently continuing a practice the nurse believes is outdated ignores accountability for evidence-based practice.
Incorrect. Using orders to work around policy for her own clients does not address the unit-wide practice or the review process.
Correct. Shared governance is the legitimate channel for translating new evidence into unit policy.
questions.rationale: Nurses are accountable for practicing within an evidence-based environment, and nursing’s body of knowledge is continuously expanding. Accountability also requires working through legitimate structures: shared-governance practice councils, educators, and EBP committees review evidence and revise policy so that every client benefits. Changing her own practice is tempting because it acts on evidence, but it bypasses governance and leaves the outdated policy in place for everyone else.
questions.takeaway: Act on new evidence through governance—bring it to the practice council—rather than ignoring it or working around policy alone.
questions.hintContent: Which option uses the structure that gives nurses control over their practice?
questions.hintStrategy: Prefer answers that use the proper channel (governance, chain of command) over unilateral action or passive acceptance.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A charge nurse is reviewing accountability with new RNs. Which statements by the new RNs reflect accurate understanding? Select all that apply.
options: “If I delegate vital signs, I am still answerable for acting on the results.”
“Once I give handoff, I am no longer accountable for omissions on my shift.”
“I am accountable for what I fail to do as well as for what I do.”
“If a provider orders a treatment, only the provider answers for the outcome.”
“I need to be able to explain the reasoning behind my nursing decisions.”
optionRationales: Correct. Delegation transfers a task, not the RN’s accountability for interpreting and acting on the data.
Incorrect. An omission that occurred during the shift remains the nurse’s accountability after handoff; it must be disclosed and reported.
Correct. Accountability covers omissions such as missed assessments or unreported findings.
Incorrect. Nurses are independently accountable for their own judgments, including questioning an unsafe order.
Correct. Accountability means being answerable for decisions, which requires sound, explainable reasoning.
questions.rationale: Accountability is answerability for one’s judgments, actions, and omissions. The RN who delegates keeps accountability for following up; the nurse who carries out an order keeps accountability for recognizing and questioning one that is unsafe; and an omission does not disappear at shift change. Being accountable means being able to explain, with data and evidence, why a decision was made.
questions.takeaway: Accountability includes omissions, delegated tasks, and the reasoning behind every nursing decision—and it does not end at handoff or with a provider’s order.
questions.hintContent: Accountability travels with the nurse’s judgment, not with the task or the paperwork.
questions.hintStrategy: In SATA, test each statement against one principle: can accountability be transferred? If a statement says it can, it is false.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse notices that a coworker, who is also a close friend, is slurring words and smells of alcohol while preparing medications for her clients. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Report the coworker directly to the state board of nursing.
Stop the coworker from giving medications and notify the charge nurse.
Encourage the coworker privately to seek treatment after this shift ends.
Watch the coworker closely and double-check each medication given.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Board reporting may follow under policy and law, but the immediate priority is protecting clients now.
Correct. Removing the impaired nurse from client care and notifying the charge nurse or supervisor protects clients immediately and starts the proper process.
Incorrect. Waiting until after the shift leaves clients at risk from an impaired nurse.
Incorrect. Supervising an impaired nurse still allows her to provide unsafe care and does not address the impairment.
questions.rationale: The nurse’s primary commitment is to the client, even when friendship makes action painful. An impaired nurse must be removed from client care immediately, and the charge nurse or supervisor is notified so the facility’s fitness-for-duty process and any required board reporting follow. Board reporting is tempting because impairment is a reportable conduct issue, but it does not stop the coworker from giving medications in the next few minutes.
questions.takeaway: Protect clients first: stop an apparently impaired colleague from providing care and notify the supervisor immediately.
questions.hintContent: Who is at risk in the next five minutes?
questions.hintStrategy: For ‘first’ items, pick the action that removes the immediate danger; reporting to outside bodies usually comes later.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control

questions.stem: Ten minutes before the end of her shift, a nurse realizes she did not perform the neurovascular check ordered 2 hours ago for a client with a new leg cast. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Perform the neurovascular check now and compare it with the baseline.
Chart the check at the scheduled time using the last recorded findings.
Ask the oncoming nurse to perform the check whenever time allows.
Report the omission to the charge nurse before seeing the client.
optionRationales: Correct. The client may have developed compartment syndrome or impaired circulation; assessing now addresses the risk created by the omission.
Incorrect. Charting a check that was not performed is falsification and could hide a deterioration.
Incorrect. Deferring an overdue assessment of a high-risk client delays recognition of a possible emergency.
Incorrect. The omission must be reported, but the client’s possible neurovascular compromise takes priority.
questions.rationale: Accountability includes omissions, and the first step in owning an omission is to remove the risk it created. A missed neurovascular check on a new cast could hide compartment syndrome, so the nurse assesses circulation, sensation, motion, pain, and swelling now. Afterward she documents the actual time, reports the omission to the charge nurse, and includes it in handoff. Reporting first is tempting because it is honest, but assessment of a potentially compromised limb comes before paperwork or notification.
questions.takeaway: When you discover an omission, first assess the client for harm, then document truthfully and report.
questions.hintContent: What could have happened to the client’s limb during the missed interval?
questions.hintStrategy: Assess before you report when a delayed assessment could be hiding an emergency.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential

questions.stem: Which situation is the best example of professional (collective) autonomy rather than individual nursing autonomy?
options: A nurse repositions an immobile client every 2 hours to protect the skin.
A nurse withholds a scheduled laxative because the client has diarrhea.
A board of nursing adopts a rule describing RN delegation responsibilities.
A nurse independently begins fall-prevention teaching with a client.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Repositioning is an independent nursing intervention—individual autonomy.
Incorrect. Holding a dose based on assessment is an individual clinical judgment.
Correct. A board defining practice through rules is the profession regulating itself—professional autonomy.
Incorrect. Initiating teaching is an independent nursing action within the individual nurse’s scope.
questions.rationale: Professional autonomy belongs to nursing as a whole: self-regulation, setting standards, formulating policy, and legal authority vested in boards of nursing. Individual autonomy is the nurse’s freedom to make and carry out independent clinical decisions within scope. Three options describe individual nurses acting independently at the bedside, which is why they all feel ‘autonomous’; only the board rule represents the profession regulating its members.
questions.takeaway: Profession-level standard setting and board rules = professional autonomy; bedside independent judgments = individual autonomy.
questions.hintContent: Is the actor an individual nurse or the profession’s regulatory structure?
questions.hintStrategy: When three options share a feature and one differs, the different one is often the answer in a ‘best example’ item.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A charge nurse is redesigning workflow so that RNs on the unit can practice at the top of their license. Which RN activities should the plan protect time for? Select all that apply.
options: Coordinating safe handoffs and transfers between units
Evaluating clients’ responses to newly started medications
Restocking linen and supply carts each morning
Teaching a client with a new colostomy before discharge
Escorting stable clients by wheelchair to the hospital exit
optionRationales: Correct. Facilitating safe transitions is a core RN responsibility within top-of-license practice.
Correct. Evaluation requires nursing judgment and is an RN accountability.
Incorrect. Restocking supplies does not require nursing education and can be done by support staff.
Correct. Initial client teaching is an RN function requiring assessment of learning needs.
Incorrect. Escorting a stable client is a task trained support staff can perform.
questions.rationale: Top-of-license practice frees RNs to do work requiring their education, judgment, and legal scope: outcomes-focused care, coordinating safe transitions, evaluating responses, and teaching. Tasks that do not require nursing judgment—restocking and routine transport of stable clients—should be done by others so RN time is not consumed by them. Protecting RN-only work is also a form of advocating for nurses’ autonomy.
questions.takeaway: Protect RN time for assessment, evaluation, teaching, and safe transitions; shift non-judgment tasks to other team members.
questions.hintContent: Which activities would be unsafe or illegal for a non-RN to perform?
questions.hintStrategy: In delegation-flavored SATA, sort each option into ‘requires RN judgment’ vs ‘routine task.’
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A bed is urgently needed, and the nurse manager asks the nurse to discharge a client now. The client, newly prescribed insulin, still cannot draw up or inject a dose correctly. Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: “I’ll give her written instructions, and she can call with any questions.”
“I’ll discharge her now and ask home health to teach her within a week.”
“I’ll have her daughter sign that she will supervise the injections.”
“She can’t inject safely yet; I’ll notify the provider and keep teaching.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Written instructions do not ensure a client who failed the return demonstration can safely give insulin tonight.
Incorrect. The client may need insulin before home health visits; discharge now leaves an unsafe gap.
Incorrect. A signature does not verify that the daughter can perform or supervise injections safely.
Correct. The nurse’s primary commitment is to client safety; she informs the provider of the unmet discharge criterion and completes teaching or arranges a safe alternative.
questions.rationale: The ANA Code places the nurse’s primary commitment with the client, and accountability for safe transitions includes verifying that a client can safely perform essential self-care before leaving. A client who cannot inject insulin is at risk of hypo- or hyperglycemia within hours. The nurse communicates the safety concern to the provider and continues teaching, or arranges a safe alternative such as a trained caregiver who demonstrates competence. Home health referral is tempting because it is a real resource, but it does not cover the doses due before the first visit.
questions.takeaway: Bed pressure never outweighs a client’s safety at discharge; verify essential self-care skills and escalate unmet criteria.
questions.hintContent: What will happen at the client’s next insulin dose if she goes home now?
questions.hintStrategy: When institutional pressure conflicts with client safety, choose the option that keeps the client safe and communicates the concern.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse is explaining to students how governance gives nurses control over their practice, self-discipline, and working conditions. Which examples illustrate governance? Select all that apply.
options: Bedside nurses on a practice council vote to revise the fall-prevention policy
The board of nursing disciplines a nurse who diverted controlled substances
A professional nursing organization advocates for safe-staffing legislation
The finance office sets the unit’s supply budget without nursing input
A physician decides which tasks are within nursing’s scope on the unit
optionRationales: Correct. Shared governance gives bedside nurses decision-making authority over practice.
Correct. Self-discipline of the profession through the board of nursing is part of governance.
Correct. Professional organizations shape the political and economic arrangements that affect nurses’ working conditions.
Incorrect. A decision made about nursing without nursing participation is the opposite of professional governance.
Incorrect. Nursing scope is defined by the Nurse Practice Act and board of nursing, not by another discipline.
questions.rationale: Governance is the structure through which professionals control their own affairs—practice, self-discipline, and working conditions—through social, political, and economic arrangements. Shared-governance councils, board discipline, and professional organizations’ advocacy are all governance. Decisions made about nursing by others, without nursing involvement, are not.
questions.takeaway: Governance = nurses controlling their practice, discipline, and working conditions through councils, boards, and professional organizations.
questions.hintContent: Ask who holds the decision-making power in each example.
questions.hintStrategy: In SATA, eliminate options where someone outside nursing controls nursing’s affairs.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse is completing an admission assessment for a 52-year-old client with a gastrointestinal diagnosis and a history of chronic back pain. The client says, “I’m doing fine,” while grimacing, gripping the side rails, and trembling. Blood pressure is 164/96 mm Hg, and heart rate is 108/min. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Document the client’s report of being fine and continue to the next client.
Notify the provider that the client is declining pain medication.
Ask the client to describe what she is feeling and rate any pain.
Administer the PRN opioid ordered for moderate to severe pain.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Documenting only the verbal report ignores incongruent cues and leaves the assessment incomplete.
Incorrect. The client has not declined anything yet; the nurse needs assessment data before calling.
Correct. The nonverbal cues and vital signs conflict with ‘fine,’ so the nurse completes the assessment by exploring the client’s experience and pain.
Incorrect. Medicating before assessing pain, its cause, and the client’s preferences skips assessment and may not match what the client is experiencing.
questions.rationale: Accountability for comfort begins with a complete assessment, especially when words and cues disagree. Grimacing, guarding, trembling, hypertension, and tachycardia suggest pain or distress that the client is minimizing, so the nurse explores and quantifies it before leaving the room. Administering the PRN opioid is tempting because pain seems likely, but intervention without assessment ignores other causes and the client’s fears about medication.
questions.takeaway: When a client’s words and cues conflict, complete the assessment before acting or leaving the room.
questions.hintContent: The verbal report and the objective cues do not match.
questions.hintStrategy: Assess before you act unless there is an emergency; look for the option that gathers the missing data.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort

questions.stem: After assessment, a client with severe pain says, “I don’t want any narcotics. I’m scared I’ll end up addicted.” Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: “Tell me more about your concerns so we can find options that work for you.”
“You won’t get addicted; that risk is basically zero while you are in the hospital.”
“Then I’ll document that you are refusing pain management for this shift.”
“Your provider ordered this medicine, so you really should take it as prescribed.”
optionRationales: Correct. An open-ended, therapeutic response explores the fear and keeps the nurse working toward acceptable relief.
Incorrect. False reassurance dismisses the concern and is not accurate; risk is low but not zero.
Incorrect. Accepting the refusal without exploring it or offering alternatives abandons accountability for comfort.
Incorrect. Pressuring the client disregards autonomy and does not address the fear.
questions.rationale: Respecting a refusal is different from abandoning the problem. Untreated pain causes physiologic stress responses—elevated blood pressure, impaired healing, heightened anxiety—so the accountable nurse explores fears, educates, and offers non-opioid and nonpharmacologic alternatives while honoring the client’s informed choice. Documenting a refusal is tempting because it respects autonomy, but on its own it leaves the client in pain without exploring options.
questions.takeaway: When a client refuses pain medication, explore the reason and pursue acceptable alternatives rather than simply acquiescing.
questions.hintContent: Which response opens the conversation instead of closing it?
questions.hintStrategy: In ‘best response’ items, choose the therapeutic, open-ended response; eliminate false reassurance, pressure, and responses that end the discussion.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort

questions.stem: An RN is planning care for a medical unit with a nursing assistant (NA) whose competence for routine tasks has been verified. Which tasks can the RN delegate to the NA? Select all that apply.
options: Measuring and recording intake and output for a client with stable heart failure
Straining all urine for a client with renal calculi and saving any stones
Teaching a client to use an incentive spirometer for the first time
Assessing a client who reports new shortness of breath
Ambulating a client who has walked independently in the hall since yesterday
Evaluating whether a client’s pain decreased after a PRN analgesic
optionRationales: Correct. Measuring I&O for a stable client is a routine, predictable task; the RN interprets the results.
Correct. Straining urine is a routine task when the RN gives clear directions about saving stones and what to report.
Incorrect. Initial teaching is an RN responsibility.
Incorrect. A new symptom requires RN assessment; the client is not stable.
Correct. Ambulating a stable client with a predictable response is appropriate to delegate.
Incorrect. Evaluating the effectiveness of an intervention requires nursing judgment.
questions.rationale: The RN may delegate routine tasks for stable clients with predictable outcomes when the NA is competent and receives clear directions. The RN never delegates assessment, initial teaching, evaluation, or the care of clients with new or changing conditions. The pain-relief item is tempting because an NA can ask for a pain rating, but deciding whether the intervention worked is evaluation, which stays with the nurse.
questions.takeaway: Delegate routine tasks for stable clients; keep assessment, teaching, evaluation, and unstable clients with the RN.
questions.hintContent: Look for verbs: measure, strain, and ambulate vs teach, assess, and evaluate.
questions.hintStrategy: Remember EAT—Evaluate, Assess, Teach stay with the RN—then check whether the client is stable.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: An RN assigned an LPN to strain all urine for a client with suspected kidney stones. The LPN reports, “He voided 30 mL a few minutes ago. I charted it and emptied the urinal without straining it.” Which statement by the RN reflects accurate understanding of accountability?
options: “Because you did the task, the error is entirely your responsibility.”
“We each have accountability; I need to clarify directions and follow up.”
“Because I assigned the task, the error is entirely my responsibility alone.”
“Neither of us is accountable, because one missed void is not likely harmful.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. The LPN is accountable for performance, but the RN retains accountability for communication, supervision, and the outcome.
Correct. The LPN answers for performing the task correctly; the RN answers for appropriate assignment, clear directions, supervision, and follow-up.
Incorrect. The LPN is a licensed professional who is also accountable for her own actions.
Incorrect. Accountability does not depend on whether harm occurred; a missed stone can delay diagnosis.
questions.rationale: When an RN assigns or delegates, the person performing the task is accountable for doing it correctly, and the RN retains accountability for the decision, the directions (strain every void), supervision, and evaluation. The accountable RN reinforces instructions, notifies the provider if the missed specimen affects the plan, documents factually, and follows the facility’s reporting process. The statement that the error is “entirely my responsibility alone” is tempting because it sounds responsible, but it ignores the LPN’s own professional accountability.
questions.takeaway: After assigning or delegating, the RN remains accountable for directions, supervision, and outcomes, and the person performing the task is accountable for doing it correctly.
questions.hintContent: Accountability is shared between the person who directs and the person who performs; it is not all-or-nothing.
questions.hintStrategy: Be wary of absolute words such as ‘entirely’ and ‘neither’ in accountability items.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A 79-year-old client with a history of heart failure is admitted with renal colic. Orders include 0.9% sodium chloride at 500 mL/hr. Before starting the infusion, the nurse auscultates fine crackles in both lung bases, and SpO2 is 92% on room air. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Start the infusion at the ordered rate and recheck the lungs in 1 hour.
Start the infusion at 100 mL/hr until the provider returns the call.
Ask the pharmacist to change the rate to one safe for heart failure.
Contact the provider to clarify the rate before starting the infusion.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Starting a high-volume infusion in a client with crackles and heart failure risks fluid overload.
Incorrect. Independently changing the ordered rate is outside nursing scope; the order must be clarified.
Incorrect. The pharmacist can advise, but the prescriber must change the order.
Correct. The nurse questions an order that appears unsafe for this client before implementing it, sharing assessment data and current evidence.
questions.rationale: Accountability for evidence-based practice and safety requires the nurse to question an order that conflicts with the client’s condition or current evidence. Large fluid boluses are rarely effective for stone passage, and an older adult with heart failure and crackles is at high risk of fluid overload. The nurse holds the infusion, calls the prescriber with SBAR, and implements the clarified order. Starting at a lower rate is tempting because it seems safer, but it is an independent change to a medical order.
questions.takeaway: Clarify an order that appears unsafe for the client before implementing it; do not change it on your own.
questions.hintContent: Consider the client’s age, history, and lung findings against the ordered volume.
questions.hintStrategy: When an order and the client’s data conflict, the first action is usually to clarify with the prescriber—not to implement, modify, or go around it.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A client with renal colic has an order for hydromorphone 1–4 mg IV every 1 hour PRN for severe pain. The client received 1 mg 1 hour ago and now rates pain 8/10. The client is awake and alert, with respirations 18/min and SpO2 97% on room air. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Give a dose within the ordered range per policy and reassess in 15–30 minutes.
Withhold further opioid doses because the first dose did not relieve the pain.
Give 4 mg now and repeat 4 mg in 30 minutes if pain is still high.
Notify the provider that the order is ineffective before giving another dose.
optionRationales: Correct. The order and timing allow another dose; the nurse selects a dose by assessment and policy and reassesses at the expected peak effect.
Incorrect. Inadequate relief from the lowest dose is a reason to titrate within the range, not to withhold analgesia.
Incorrect. A repeat dose 30 minutes later violates the every-1-hour frequency and would give 8 mg in 1 hour, double the 4-mg maximum the order allows per dosing interval.
Incorrect. The order has not yet been used fully; the provider is notified if relief remains inadequate after appropriate titration.
questions.rationale: With a range order, the nurse is accountable for an accurate assessment, a dose within the range and the frequency allowed by the order and policy, and close monitoring of pain, sedation, and respirations. The nurse is not accountable for a drug’s pharmacologic failure when that process is followed, but is accountable for reassessing and notifying the provider if relief remains inadequate. Calling the provider first is tempting, but the order already allows titration for this alert client with stable respirations. Repeating a full dose in 30 minutes breaks both limits of the order: the dose ceiling and the dosing interval.
questions.takeaway: Use range orders by assessing, selecting an allowed dose, reassessing at peak effect, and escalating if relief remains inadequate.
questions.hintContent: Check what the order and the client’s current status allow right now.
questions.hintStrategy: Verify every number in the options against the order; eliminate any that exceed the prescribed range.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies

questions.stem: A nurse educator is discussing medication accountability with new nurses. Which statement by a new nurse indicates a need for further teaching?
options: “I must assess pain and sedation before I choose a dose within a range order.”
“I need to reassess after the dose and report it if pain relief is inadequate.”
“If an ordered opioid dose doesn’t relieve pain, the failure is my fault.”
“An older client may need a lower starting dose and closer sedation monitoring.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. This is accurate: assessment guides dose selection within a range.
Incorrect. This is accurate: reassessment and escalation are nursing accountabilities.
Correct. This statement needs correction: the nurse is accountable for a sound process, not for an individual client’s pharmacologic response.
Incorrect. This is accurate: older adults have greater risk of opioid-induced respiratory depression.
questions.rationale: Nurses answer for their process: accurate assessment, safe administration within the order, monitoring, reassessment, and escalation when relief is inadequate. They are not accountable for a medication’s failure to work in a particular client when that process is followed. The other statements describe correct practice, including the age-related caution, which is tempting to pick only if the learner forgets that older adults need closer monitoring.
questions.takeaway: You are accountable for your medication process—assess, give correctly, monitor, reassess, escalate—not for the drug’s biology.
questions.hintContent: Separate what the nurse controls from what the drug does.
questions.hintStrategy: For ‘needs further teaching,’ find the one statement that misstates where accountability lies.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies

questions.stem: A provider orders potassium chloride 20 mEq IV push for a client with a potassium level of 3.1 mEq/L. When the nurse questions the route, the provider says, “Just push it slowly—I’ve done it before.” Which action should the nurse take next?
options: Give the dose by slow IV push over 10 minutes to reduce the risk.
Withhold the dose, tell the provider, and notify the charge nurse.
Ask another nurse who is more comfortable to give the dose.
Document the provider’s statement and then give the dose as ordered.
optionRationales: Incorrect. IV push potassium can cause fatal dysrhythmias regardless of speed; it must be diluted and infused.
Correct. The nurse refuses to carry out an unsafe order, informs the prescriber, and escalates through the chain of command.
Incorrect. Handing an unsafe order to a colleague does not make it safe and shifts the danger rather than resolving it.
Incorrect. Documentation does not protect the client or the nurse from carrying out an order known to be dangerous.
questions.rationale: Nurses are individually accountable for their actions, so an order that would endanger the client must not be carried out even if the prescriber insists. The nurse withholds the dose, informs the prescriber it will not be given as written, and escalates immediately—charge nurse, nursing supervisor, then medical director—while documenting the facts. Documenting and then giving the dose is tempting because it seems to transfer responsibility, but the nurse remains accountable for giving a lethal medication.
questions.takeaway: If a prescriber refuses to change an unsafe order, do not carry it out—inform the prescriber, escalate through the chain of command, and document.
questions.hintContent: Potassium chloride is never given by IV push.
questions.hintStrategy: An unsafe order is never made safe by documentation or by handing it to someone else; look for refusal plus escalation.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse in the emergency department is caring for a 3-year-old with sharply demarcated burns in a stocking pattern on both feet. The parent states the child “stepped into hot bath water.” Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Document the location, size, and pattern of the burns objectively
Report the suspected abuse to child protective services
Confront the parent about the inconsistency in the explanation
Wait until the provider confirms abuse before making any report
Record the parent’s explanation using the parent’s own words
Tell the parent the child will be removed from the home today
optionRationales: Correct. Objective, specific documentation supports the report and the child’s care.
Correct. Nurses must report reasonable suspicion of child abuse to the designated child protective agency (in North Carolina, the county department of social services).
Incorrect. Confrontation can escalate risk to the child and staff; investigation is the agency’s role.
Incorrect. The legal duty is to report suspicion; proof or a provider’s confirmation is not required.
Correct. Quoting the caregiver’s explanation preserves accurate information for investigators.
Incorrect. Nurses do not determine custody; that decision belongs to child protective services and the courts.
questions.rationale: A stocking-pattern immersion burn with an explanation that does not fit the injury is a classic cue of abuse. Nurses have a legal and ethical mandatory duty to report suspected child abuse; they report suspicion, document objectively (including the caregiver’s exact words), and protect the child, but they do not investigate, confront, or make custody decisions. Waiting for the provider’s confirmation is tempting because it feels more certain, but it delays a report the nurse is required to make. (In North Carolina, the report goes to the county department of social services, and any person with cause to suspect child maltreatment must report.)
questions.takeaway: Report suspected child abuse to the designated agency based on reasonable suspicion, and document objectively—do not wait for proof or confront the caregiver.
questions.hintContent: Does the mechanism described match the burn pattern?
questions.hintStrategy: In mandatory-reporting SATA, select documentation and reporting actions; reject confronting, investigating, waiting, or deciding custody.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: During an admission for pneumonia, a 68-year-old client whose spouse died recently says, “It doesn’t really matter what happens to me anymore.” Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: “Many people feel down when they are sick; you will feel better soon.”
“Let’s focus on your breathing treatments now and talk about this later.”
“I’ll ask the chaplain to stop by and visit with you this afternoon.”
“Are you having thoughts of ending your life or hurting yourself?”
optionRationales: Incorrect. False reassurance dismisses a possible warning sign of suicidal ideation.
Incorrect. Postponing the discussion delays assessment of a possible safety risk.
Incorrect. A chaplain referral may help later, but it does not assess immediate suicide risk.
Correct. Asking directly about suicidal thoughts assesses risk; asking does not increase the likelihood of suicide.
questions.rationale: Nurses are accountable for screening every client for suicide risk on admission and for staying alert to verbalized warning signs. Recent loss, older age, illness, and hopeless statements are risk cues, and the appropriate response is to ask directly about suicidal thoughts, plan, and means. The chaplain referral is tempting because it addresses grief and spiritual needs, but referral comes after the nurse determines whether the client is safe.
questions.takeaway: When a client makes a hopeless statement, ask directly about suicidal thoughts before offering reassurance or referrals.
questions.hintContent: The statement may be a verbal warning sign; what assessment is needed?
questions.hintStrategy: Assessment before intervention: choose the option that gathers safety-critical data first.
questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity

questions.stem: A nurse who works on an oncology unit wakes up with a temperature of 38.4°C (101.1°F), a sore throat, and body aches 2 hours before her shift. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Notify the supervisor and employee health that she cannot work.
Wear a surgical mask all shift and avoid clients who are neutropenic.
Take an antipyretic before the shift and monitor her temperature.
Work the shift but ask to care only for clients not on chemotherapy.
optionRationales: Correct. Self-awareness of personal illness and exposure is part of infection-prevention accountability; a febrile nurse should not work with immunocompromised clients.
Incorrect. A mask does not make it safe to work while febrile with a likely transmissible illness on an oncology unit.
Incorrect. Masking a fever with medication hides the illness without reducing transmission risk.
Incorrect. Many oncology clients are immunocompromised regardless of current treatment, and staff and visitors are also at risk.
questions.rationale: The infection row of the related-concepts matrix makes nurses accountable for protecting clients whose immune systems are compromised, including through self-awareness of their own exposures and illness. A nurse with fever and respiratory symptoms should notify the supervisor and employee health and follow exclusion policy. Wearing a mask is the most tempting option because it is a real infection-control measure, but it does not make working while febrile acceptable on a unit full of immunocompromised clients.
questions.takeaway: A nurse with a fever or likely transmissible illness stays home and notifies the supervisor and employee health.
questions.hintContent: Who on this unit is most vulnerable to her illness?
questions.hintStrategy: In infection-control items, prevent exposure at the source before relying on PPE.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control

questions.stem: The RN is making assignments for an LPN on a medical-surgical unit. Review the exhibit. Which client should the RN assign to the LPN?

rows: COPD; SpO2 dropped from 92% to 86% over the past hour; increased work of breathing
First unit of packed red blood cells started 10 minutes ago
Postoperative day 2 hip arthroplasty; stable vital signs; needs scheduled oral analgesic and reinforcement of incentive spirometer use
Admitted 1 hour ago in sickle cell crisis; pain 9/10; initial pain management plan pending

options: Client A, with COPD and a falling oxygen saturation
Client B, who is receiving a first unit of blood
Client C, on day 2 after hip arthroplasty
Client D, newly admitted in sickle cell crisis
optionRationales: Incorrect. A falling SpO2 with increased work of breathing is an unstable, changing condition requiring RN assessment.
Incorrect. The first 15 minutes of a transfusion carry the highest risk of reaction and require RN monitoring and judgment.
Correct. A stable client with predictable needs—scheduled oral medication and reinforcement of previously taught teaching—fits LPN scope.
Incorrect. A new admission in crisis needs RN assessment and an initial plan of care.
questions.rationale: The RN assigns to the LPN clients who are stable with predictable outcomes and keeps clients with new, changing, or high-risk situations. The LPN can administer scheduled oral medications and reinforce teaching the RN has already done. The client receiving blood is tempting because LPNs may assist with some transfusion-related care in certain settings, but the early transfusion period requires RN assessment for reactions, and assignment rules remain the RN’s accountability.
questions.takeaway: Assign stable, predictable clients to the LPN; keep new admissions, early transfusions, and changing conditions with the RN.
questions.hintContent: Which client’s condition is least likely to change suddenly?
questions.hintStrategy: Sort clients into stable/predictable vs new/unstable/high-risk; the stable one goes to the LPN.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse manager is using a Just Culture framework to review several medication events. Which pairings of event and response are consistent with Just Culture? Select all that apply.
options: A nurse selects the wrong client from two look-alike names on a list — console the nurse and fix the system
A nurse routinely bypasses barcode scanning because it is slow — coach the nurse about the risk
A nurse comes to work intoxicated and gives medications — console the nurse as a human error
A nurse knowingly leaves a sedated client unmonitored after repeated warnings — apply disciplinary action
A nurse transposes digits while transcribing during a heavy workload — treat it as reckless behavior
optionRationales: Correct. An unintended slip in a confusing system is human error; the response is consoling and redesigning the system.
Correct. Drifting into an unsafe shortcut whose risk is not recognized is at-risk behavior; the response is coaching.
Incorrect. Working while intoxicated is a conscious disregard of substantial risk (and a conduct issue), not a human error.
Correct. Conscious disregard of a known, unjustifiable risk is reckless behavior, which warrants disciplinary action.
Incorrect. An unintended transcription slip is human error, not reckless behavior.
questions.rationale: Just Culture holds people accountable for their choices while recognizing that most errors arise from system weaknesses. Human error (slips and lapses) calls for consoling the person and fixing the system; at-risk behavior (unsafe shortcuts whose risk is underestimated) calls for coaching; reckless behavior (conscious disregard of substantial, unjustifiable risk) warrants discipline. Impairment on duty is not treated as a simple human error and is also a reportable conduct issue.
questions.takeaway: Just Culture: console human error, coach at-risk behavior, and sanction reckless behavior.
questions.hintContent: Classify each event by the person’s choice: unintended slip, risky drift, or conscious disregard.
questions.hintStrategy: For classification SATA, decide each pairing independently against the definitions.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control

questions.stem: A nurse plans to teach a client about newly prescribed warfarin before discharge. The client received IV morphine 20 minutes ago, is drowsy, and says, “Just leave the papers with me.” Which action by the nurse is best?
options: Proceed with the full teaching and leave the written materials at the bedside.
Postpone teaching until the client is alert and ready to learn.
Ask the client to sign the form stating the teaching was completed.
Ask the LPN to complete the warfarin teaching after the next medication pass.
optionRationales: Incorrect. A drowsy client is not ready to learn, so the teaching is unlikely to be retained.
Correct. Assessing readiness to learn comes before teaching; the nurse reschedules and later confirms understanding with teach-back.
Incorrect. A signature documents an event, not learning; it would misrepresent what the client understands.
Incorrect. Initial teaching on a new high-risk medication is an RN responsibility; the LPN may reinforce it later.
questions.rationale: Accountability for teaching requires assessing a client’s learning needs, learning style, and readiness before teaching. Recent opioid administration and drowsiness signal that the client cannot absorb information about a high-alert medication.
