The nurse postpones teaching, plans a time when the client is alert (and, with consent, includes a support person), and evaluates learning with teach-back. Leaving written materials is tempting because it seems efficient, but it does not meet the standard for a new anticoagulant.
questions.takeaway: Assess readiness to learn before teaching; a drowsy, medicated client is not ready.
questions.hintContent: What must be true about the learner before teaching can succeed?
questions.hintStrategy: In teaching items, choose the option that addresses readiness and verifies learning; reject options that simply document or hand off.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A client on the first day after abdominal surgery rated pain 3/10 at 0800. At 1100, the client is splinting the incision and rates pain 7/10. Which actions are consistent with the nurse’s accountability for comfort? Select all that apply.
options: Wait for the next scheduled shift assessment to reassess comfort
Assess pain location, quality, and the surgical site
Ask the nursing assistant to judge whether the analgesic was effective
Implement ordered analgesic and nonpharmacologic comfort measures
Document the pain rating, interventions, and the client’s response
optionRationales: Incorrect. Once-per-shift assessment is a minimum; a change in comfort requires prompt reassessment.
Correct. A significant change in pain warrants a focused assessment of the pain and the incision.
Incorrect. Evaluating effectiveness requires nursing judgment and cannot be delegated to a nursing assistant.
Correct. The nurse provides effective interventions to restore comfort.
Correct. Documenting the comfort level and every intervention is part of comfort accountability.
questions.rationale: The comfort row of the matrix makes the nurse accountable for assessing comfort at least once per shift or more often as the condition requires, reporting deviations, intervening effectively, and documenting the comfort level and all interventions. A rise from 3/10 to 7/10 with splinting is a change that requires assessment (including the surgical site, to rule out a complication), intervention, reassessment, and documentation. Asking the NA to judge effectiveness is tempting for efficiency, but evaluation remains an RN function.
questions.takeaway: A change in comfort calls for prompt assessment, intervention, reassessment, and documentation—not waiting for the next routine check.
questions.hintContent: ‘At least once per shift’ is a minimum, not a schedule to wait for.
questions.hintStrategy: In SATA, eliminate options that delay assessment or delegate evaluation.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort

questions.stem: An RN with 10 years of adult medical-surgical experience is floated to labor and delivery and told she will care for a laboring client receiving an oxytocin infusion. She has never worked in obstetrics. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Accept the assignment and ask the client to call if her contractions change.
Refuse to float and remain on her home unit for the rest of the shift.
Accept the assignment and review the oxytocin protocol during the shift.
Before report, tell the charge nurse about the gap and ask for a safe role.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Relying on the client to detect complications of oxytocin transfers the nurse’s monitoring responsibility to the client.
Incorrect. Flatly refusing ignores the staffing need and skips negotiating a role within her competence.
Incorrect. ‘Learning as she goes’ with a high-alert infusion is exactly the guessing the first rule of competence warns against.
Correct. She communicates her limitation before accepting the clients and negotiates a role within her competence.
questions.rationale: A nurse must self-assess competence and must not accept an independent assignment requiring specialized knowledge and skills she lacks. Oxytocin infusions require fetal heart rate and contraction monitoring skills a medical-surgical nurse has not been validated on. The accountable action is to tell the charge nurse before accepting report and negotiate tasks within her competence, a buddy role, or reassignment. Flat refusal is tempting because it protects the client from her inexperience, but negotiating a safe role protects the client while still meeting the unit’s need.
questions.takeaway: When floated beyond your competence, say so before accepting report and negotiate a safe role—don’t guess, and don’t just walk away.
questions.hintContent: Timing and communication matter: when and to whom should she raise the concern?
questions.hintStrategy: In floating items, the best answer usually names the competence gap to the person making assignments and proposes a safe alternative.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse with 4 years of experience on a cardiac unit begins planning each client’s discharge needs at admission. She says, “When a heart failure client suddenly can’t lie flat, I go see them right away,” and she recognizes how individual findings fit together into a whole picture. Which of Benner’s stages best describes this nurse?
options: Proficient
Competent
Expert
Advanced beginner
optionRationales: Correct. Perceiving situations as wholes, using maxims, and focusing on long-term goals (about 3–5 years) define the proficient stage.
Incorrect. The competent nurse (about 2–3 years) plans deliberately and organizes well but does not yet perceive situations as wholes guided by maxims.
Incorrect. The expert no longer relies on maxims to connect understanding with action and acts intuitively.
Incorrect. The advanced beginner recognizes recurring aspects but needs help setting priorities.
questions.rationale: Benner’s proficient nurse, typically with about 3–5 years of experience, perceives situations as wholes, uses maxims (‘a heart failure client who suddenly can’t lie flat needs to be seen now’) as guides, and focuses on long-term goals such as discharge. The expert is the most tempting distractor because this nurse is clearly skilled, but experts no longer need maxims and act from deep intuitive grasp.
questions.takeaway: Maxims plus whole-picture perception and long-term goals = proficient; intuition without needing maxims = expert.
questions.hintContent: Notice the nurse’s use of a rule of thumb (a maxim).
questions.hintStrategy: Match the most distinctive behavior in the stem to the single stage that owns it.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A preceptor is planning the third week of orientation for a new graduate nurse. Which approach is most appropriate for the new graduate’s developmental stage?
options: Assign the most unstable clients so the new graduate learns quickly.
Allow the new graduate to work independently and review at shift end.
Assign stable clients and help the new graduate set priorities.
Limit the new graduate to vital signs and hygiene for the first month.
optionRationales: Incorrect. An advanced beginner is not ready to manage the most unstable clients and needs support with complex demands.
Incorrect. Independent practice without ongoing support is premature during orientation.
Correct. Advanced beginners recognize recurring aspects of care but need help prioritizing; stable assignments with coaching match that stage.
Incorrect. Restricting a licensed RN to assistive tasks does not develop RN competence or use the RN’s scope.
questions.rationale: In Benner’s model, the new graduate is an advanced beginner who shows marginally acceptable performance and recognizes meaningful recurring aspects of situations from limited experience. Such nurses need help setting priorities when demands compete. A preceptor builds competence by assigning stable clients and coaching prioritization, increasing complexity as skill grows. Throwing a new graduate into the most unstable assignment is tempting as ‘learning by doing,’ but it exceeds current competence and endangers clients.
questions.takeaway: Advanced beginners need stable assignments and coaching in prioritization, with complexity added as competence grows.
questions.hintContent: Which Benner stage is a new graduate, and what support does that stage need?
questions.hintStrategy: Match the plan to the learner’s stage; eliminate extremes that over- or under-challenge.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse educator is evaluating new nurses’ understanding of the first rule of competence. Which statement by a new nurse indicates a need for further teaching?
options: “I’ll ask my preceptor to help me the first time I access an implanted port.”
“I’m not sure this dose is right, but I think it is, so I’ll go ahead and give it.”
“This insulin infusion is high-alert, so I’ll ask for an independent double-check.”
“I haven’t used this pump before; would you help me program it correctly?”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Asking for help with a first-time procedure reflects the first rule of competence.
Correct. This statement needs correction: guessing when uncertain about a dose violates the first rule of competence—verify before giving.
Incorrect. Independent double-checks for high-alert medications are appropriate at every level of experience.
Incorrect. Acknowledging unfamiliarity with equipment and asking for help is safe practice.
questions.rationale: The first rule of competence is to ask for help whenever there is any uncertainty about the safety of an action. Saying “I don’t know” or “Would you help me?” is safer and more honorable than “I’m not sure, but I think this is right” or “I’ll figure it out as I go.” The double-check statement might look like unnecessary caution, but independent double-checks for high-alert drugs are expected of nurses at every stage.
questions.takeaway: When unsure about safety, stop and ask—never give a medication you are not sure is right.
questions.hintContent: Which nurse is guessing instead of verifying?
questions.hintStrategy: In ‘needs further teaching’ items about safety, select the statement that proceeds despite uncertainty.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control

questions.stem: A charge nurse is discussing emotional intelligence (EI) during a staff meeting. Which nurse behaviors demonstrate EI? Select all that apply.
options: Recognizing that frustration with a demanding client is delaying her response to the call light
Pausing to regain composure before responding to an angry family member
Avoiding a provider who was rude earlier instead of reporting a new abnormal finding
Asking a colleague for an objective opinion when she feels strongly about a case
Concluding that a client who calls often is “just anxious” without assessing new symptoms
optionRationales: Correct. Noticing that an emotion is influencing a clinical decision is the core of EI.
Correct. Self-regulation before responding supports professional, therapeutic communication.
Incorrect. Allowing discomfort to delay escalation of an abnormal finding is a failure of EI that endangers the client.
Correct. Seeking an outside perspective when emotions run high protects objective judgment.
Incorrect. Labeling a client based on frustration lets emotion replace assessment.
questions.rationale: Emotional intelligence is the ability to recognize, through emotional appraisal, when personal emotions rather than objective knowledge are influencing clinical decisions. EI supports problem solving and strengthens relationships with clients and colleagues. Behaviors that notice an emotion, regulate it, or check it against others’ perspectives demonstrate EI; behaviors that let fear or frustration override assessment or escalation do not.
questions.takeaway: Emotional intelligence means noticing when feelings are steering your decisions and correcting course toward objective data.
questions.hintContent: For each behavior, ask: is the nurse managing the emotion, or is the emotion managing the nurse?
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each SATA option on its own against the definition; don’t look for a pattern.
questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity

questions.stem: A client has used the call light 10 times this shift for minor requests. The client now calls and reports “a heavy pressure” in the chest. The nurse thinks, “He’s just anxious again.” Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Assess the client’s chest pressure and vital signs at the bedside.
Remind the client that he was checked on just 15 minutes ago.
Ask the nursing assistant to check on the client and report back.
Give the PRN anxiolytic that is ordered for the client’s anxiety.
optionRationales: Correct. New chest pressure is a potential emergency that requires immediate RN assessment regardless of the client’s prior behavior.
Incorrect. This dismisses a new and potentially life-threatening symptom.
Incorrect. A nursing assistant cannot assess chest pain; this is RN work.
Incorrect. Treating the symptom as anxiety before assessment could mask an acute coronary event.
questions.rationale: Problem solving requires self-awareness and emotional intelligence so that emotion does not override objective clinical judgment. The nurse’s frustration is creating an anchoring bias; new chest pressure must be assessed immediately (vital signs, symptom characteristics, and an ECG per protocol), and the provider notified. Giving the anxiolytic is tempting because it is ordered and matches the nurse’s assumption, but it treats an unverified cause and could mask cardiac ischemia.
questions.takeaway: A new symptom gets an objective assessment, no matter how often the client has called before.
questions.hintContent: Is ‘chest pressure’ a new symptom or the same as earlier requests?
questions.hintStrategy: When a stem shows the nurse’s bias, choose the option that relies on assessment data rather than the assumption.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential

questions.stem: A nurse has just finished a 12-hour shift and is asked to stay for another 8 hours. Earlier she nearly scanned the wrong client’s wristband, and she has been awake for 20 hours. Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: “I’ll stay, but I’ll drink some coffee and double-check everything.”
“I’ll stay if you give me the least acutely ill clients on the unit.”
“I’ll stay four hours and then leave whether or not relief has arrived.”
“I’m too fatigued to practice safely, but I can help find coverage.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Caffeine and extra checks do not reverse the impaired judgment caused by severe fatigue.
Incorrect. Even ‘easy’ clients can deteriorate, and a fatigued nurse may miss the change.
Incorrect. Leaving accepted clients without a proper handoff could constitute abandonment.
Correct. Monitoring her own physical well-being and declining work she cannot do safely is part of competence and ethical practice.
questions.rationale: Ethical reasoning and competence include monitoring one’s own physical and emotional well-being, because working while compromised endangers clients. A recent near miss after 20 hours awake is a clear warning that her judgment is impaired. The accountable response is to decline the extra shift honestly while helping solve the staffing problem. Staying with a lighter assignment is tempting because it seems like a compromise, but fatigue impairs recognition of deterioration in any client.
questions.takeaway: Fitness for duty is part of competence: decline extra work you cannot perform safely and help find a safe alternative.
questions.hintContent: What did the near miss reveal about her current state?
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate compromise options that still place a compromised nurse in charge of clients.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control

questions.stem: A float nurse accepted report on four clients on an unfamiliar unit. Two hours later, she realizes that one client needs tracheostomy suctioning and care, which she has never performed. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Notify the charge nurse that she has not been validated on tracheostomy care
Ask a competent nurse to perform the care or supervise her doing it
Return to her home unit because she is not competent for this unit
Continue monitoring the client’s respiratory status until help arrives
Watch an online video and then perform the tracheostomy care alone
optionRationales: Correct. Communicating the competence gap to the person responsible for assignments is the first rule of competence in action.
Correct. Having a competent nurse perform or directly supervise the skill protects the client.
Incorrect. Leaving clients she has accepted without a proper handoff could be patient abandonment.
Correct. She remains responsible for the clients she accepted and must keep monitoring the airway while help comes.
Incorrect. A video does not validate competence for an airway procedure; attempting it alone is guessing.
questions.rationale: Once a nurse accepts an assignment, she remains responsible for those clients and must not leave without a proper handoff. When she identifies a specific skill she cannot perform safely, she tells the charge nurse, arranges for a competent nurse to perform or supervise the skill, and keeps monitoring the client in the meantime. Learning from a video is tempting because it shows initiative, but watching a procedure does not establish competence for an airway intervention.
questions.takeaway: After accepting an assignment, address a skill gap by asking for help and keeping the client safe—never by leaving or guessing.
questions.hintContent: She has already accepted the clients; what does that change?
questions.hintStrategy: In competence SATA, select actions that disclose the limit, bring in competent help, and keep monitoring; reject leaving and self-teaching.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A client who speaks Vietnamese and limited English is about to have the provider explain the risks of a scheduled procedure. The client’s 14-year-old granddaughter offers to interpret. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Accept the granddaughter’s offer because the client trusts her.
Arrange for a qualified medical interpreter for the discussion.
Use gestures and simple English words to explain the procedure.
Ask a bilingual staff member from housekeeping to interpret.
optionRationales: Incorrect. A minor family member may interpret inaccurately, omit information, and is placed in an inappropriate role.
Correct. A qualified medical interpreter ensures accurate communication of risks and protects the client’s right to informed decisions.
Incorrect. Gestures and simple words cannot convey the risks and alternatives needed for informed consent.
Incorrect. Untrained bilingual staff may lack medical vocabulary and interpreter training, which risks errors and privacy breaches.
questions.rationale: Cultural competence includes strong listening skills, advocacy for the client, and ensuring communication supports informed decisions. Language barriers contribute to health disparities, so a qualified medical interpreter (in person, video, or phone) is used for health information and consent discussions. The granddaughter is the most tempting option because the client trusts her, but family members—especially minors—can misinterpret or filter information and should not interpret clinical content.
questions.takeaway: Use a qualified medical interpreter for health information and consent—not family members, minors, or untrained staff.
questions.hintContent: Who can guarantee accurate medical interpretation?
questions.hintStrategy: In diversity items, choose the option that ensures accurate communication and client rights over convenience.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A month after cultural competence training, a nurse educator observes staff nurses on the unit. Which observed actions indicate the training was effective? Select all that apply.
options: A nurse reflects on how her own beliefs about expressing pain may affect her pain assessments
A nurse asks a client which family members the client wants included in care decisions
A nurse plans a client’s meals from what most people of the client’s ethnic group usually eat
A nurse tells the team a client declines blood for religious reasons and asks about alternatives
A nurse arranges follow-up with a community clinic that serves the client’s language group
A nurse tells a client to stop a traditional herbal remedy without asking what it contains
optionRationales: Correct. Recognizing one’s own values and beliefs and how they affect care is a core element of cultural competence.
Correct. Listening and learning the client’s own rites, traditions, and decision-making preferences—by asking rather than assuming—is a core element.
Incorrect. Predicting an individual’s preferences from group membership is stereotyping; the nurse asks the client about food preferences and restrictions.
Correct. Advocating for the client’s wishes when a treatment conflicts with cultural or religious values is a core element.
Correct. Identifying community resources for follow-up care helps prevent recurrence and readmission.
Incorrect. The nurse should ask about the remedy, check it for interactions with the pharmacist or provider, and discuss it respectfully rather than dismissing it.
questions.rationale: The four core elements of cultural competence training are recognizing one’s own values and beliefs, developing listening skills and understanding cultural rites and traditions, advocating for clients’ wishes when treatments conflict with cultural values, and identifying community resources for follow-up care. Effective training shows up as behavior: self-reflection, asking the individual, advocating, and connecting to resources. Planning meals from ethnic group norms is tempting because it sounds culturally informed, but it is stereotyping. Dismissing a traditional remedy without asking ignores both the client’s values and a possible safety issue (drug–herb interactions).
questions.takeaway: Cultural competence shows up as behavior: know yourself, ask and listen, advocate, and connect to community resources, without assuming from group membership.
questions.hintContent: Match each behavior to one of the four core elements of cultural competence training.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that assume from group membership or dismiss the client’s practices without asking.
questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity

questions.stem: An experienced nurse preparing a continuous heparin infusion tells a new graduate, “You don’t need to double-check me—I’ve done hundreds of these.” Unit policy requires an independent double-check. Which response by the new graduate is best?
options: “Okay, you’re the expert; I’ll sign that the check was completed.”
“I’ll sign now, and we can review the pump settings together later.”
“Policy requires an independent check, so let’s verify it together now.”
“I’ll ask the charge nurse whether you really need a double-check on this.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Signing for a check that did not happen is falsification and removes a safeguard for a high-alert drug.
Incorrect. A check performed after the infusion starts cannot prevent a programming error.
Correct. Even experts must double-check high-risk actions; the new graduate respectfully insists on the required independent check before the infusion begins.
Incorrect. Policy already answers the question; delaying to ask the charge nurse avoids the responsibility to speak up.
questions.rationale: The safety alert states that even expert nurses continue double-checking high-risk actions such as medication doses. Heparin is a high-alert medication, and an independent double-check before the infusion starts is a system safeguard, not a judgment of skill. The new graduate should respectfully but clearly require the check now. Asking the charge nurse is tempting for a new nurse uncomfortable confronting an expert, but the policy is clear and the infusion should not start until the check is done.
questions.takeaway: Expertise never removes the need for an independent double-check of a high-alert medication.
questions.hintContent: What does the safety alert say about experts and high-risk actions?
questions.hintStrategy: In speaking-up items, choose the respectful, direct statement that preserves the safeguard before harm can occur.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control

questions.stem: At 0900, a nurse prepares a client’s scheduled oral antihypertensive. The client’s blood pressure is 88/52 mm Hg, and the client reports dizziness when sitting up. Which action by the nurse best demonstrates critical thinking?
options: Give the scheduled dose on time because it is an active order.
Give half the dose to lower the risk of further hypotension.
Give the dose and recheck the blood pressure in 1 hour.
Hold the dose, reassess the client, and notify the provider.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Giving a medication on schedule without considering the client’s current condition is task completion, not critical thinking.
Incorrect. Changing the dose independently is outside nursing scope.
Incorrect. Giving an antihypertensive to a hypotensive, dizzy client could worsen hypotension and cause a fall.
Correct. Critical thinkers inquire and investigate before acting; holding, reassessing, and notifying the provider fits the data.
questions.rationale: Critical thinking means inquiring and investigating before acting and relying on evidence rather than routine. Hypotension with dizziness makes the scheduled antihypertensive unsafe now, so the nurse holds it, reassesses (including orthostatic risk and fall precautions), and notifies the provider. Giving half the dose is tempting because it seems like a cautious middle ground, but it is an independent dose change that the nurse cannot make without an order.
questions.takeaway: Critical thinking asks whether an ordered action still makes sense for this client right now before carrying it out.
questions.hintContent: Compare the medication’s effect with the client’s current blood pressure.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that give the drug as usual or alter the dose on your own; choose hold-reassess-notify when data make a dose unsafe.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies

questions.stem: An expert nurse tells the charge nurse, “Something isn’t right with Mr. Jensen,” although each of his vital signs is still within normal limits. Review the exhibit. Which action should the charge nurse take first?
options: Perform a focused assessment of mental status, perfusion, and trends.
Document the concern and recheck vital signs at the next scheduled round.
Reassure the nurse that all vital signs remain within normal limits.
Ask the provider to order a sedative for the client’s new restlessness.
optionRationales: Correct. The expert’s intuition plus a worsening trend and new restlessness are cues to assess immediately and escalate according to findings.
Incorrect. Waiting for the next round ignores a deteriorating trend and a new mental status change.
Incorrect. Normal individual values can hide a dangerous trend; dismissing the expert’s concern delays recognition.
Incorrect. Sedating restlessness before identifying its cause could mask hypoxia or sepsis.
questions.rationale: Benner’s expert nurse uses intuitive and analytic ability—‘it felt right’—and her concern is a valid cue to investigate. The trend shows rising heart rate, respiratory rate, and temperature with falling blood pressure and new restlessness, a pattern that can signal early sepsis or other deterioration. The first action is a focused assessment (mental status, perfusion, SpO2, and trends), followed by escalation such as notifying the provider or calling a rapid response. Reassurance is tempting because each value is technically normal, but competence means looking at trends and taking expert concern seriously.
questions.takeaway: Take an expert’s ‘something isn’t right’ seriously: look at trends and assess promptly, even when single values are normal.
questions.hintContent: Look across the rows, not just at each value.
questions.hintStrategy: When an exhibit shows trends, evaluate the direction of change; assessment comes before sedation or reassurance.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential

questions.stem: A nurse with 6 years of medical-surgical experience transfers to an outpatient dialysis unit and asks how to build competence in the new specialty. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Rely on her medical-surgical experience and learn on the job without orientation.
Complete a supervised orientation with a preceptor and competency validation.
Read journal articles at home and take a full client assignment next week.
Attend one dialysis workshop and then help orient other new staff members.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Experience in one specialty does not transfer automatically; a new specialty requires orientation.
Correct. Supervised orientation with a preceptor and validated competencies is how a nurse safely builds competence in a new specialty.
Incorrect. Reading is useful but does not validate hands-on dialysis skills before an independent assignment.
Incorrect. A single workshop does not establish the competence needed to practice or to teach others.
questions.rationale: Competence is setting-specific; an experienced nurse entering a new specialty may function at an earlier Benner stage there. Strategies for strengthening competence include continuing education, workshops, peer-reviewed literature, mentorship or preceptorship, and supervised clinical orientation, with competency validation before independent practice. Reading journal articles is tempting because it is a legitimate strategy, but it is not sufficient on its own before taking a full independent assignment.
questions.takeaway: Changing specialties requires supervised orientation and validated competencies before independent practice.
questions.hintContent: Is competence transferable across specialties?
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the option that combines learning with supervised practice and validation.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse manager is completing the annual evaluation of a nurse who has worked on the same medical intensive care unit for 15 years. Which observed behaviors are consistent with Benner’s expert stage (Stage V)? Select all that apply.
options: Senses that a client is deteriorating before vital signs change and acts on it promptly
Needs the written procedure to decide what to do in most routine care situations
Requests an independent double-check before starting an insulin infusion
Switches to deliberate, step-by-step analysis when a presentation is unfamiliar
States she no longer needs to consult colleagues when she is uncertain
Relies on maxims such as “new confusion means check oxygenation” to guide actions
optionRationales: Correct. Experts act from a deep intuitive grasp of the whole situation, with fluid, flexible performance (“it felt right”), and confirm it with assessment.
Incorrect. Needing context-free rules to guide routine actions characterizes the novice.
Correct. Expert vigilance means continuing to double-check high-risk actions such as high-alert medication doses.
Correct. Experts combine highly skilled intuitive and analytic ability, using analysis when a situation is unfamiliar.
Incorrect. The first rule of competence—ask for help whenever there is uncertainty about safety—applies at every level of proficiency.
Incorrect. Using maxims as guides characterizes the proficient stage; experts no longer rely on rules, guidelines, or maxims to connect understanding to action.
questions.rationale: Benner’s expert performs fluidly and flexibly, no longer relying on rules, guidelines, or maxims to connect understanding with action, and uses highly skilled intuitive and analytic ability. Expertise does not exempt the nurse from safety practices: experts still double-check high-risk actions and still ask for help whenever they are uncertain. The maxim option is the most tempting distractor because it sounds experienced, but guidance by maxims is the hallmark of the proficient nurse; the claim that she no longer needs help violates the first rule of competence.
questions.takeaway: Experts act intuitively and analytically without needing maxims—but still double-check high-risk actions and ask for help when uncertain.
questions.hintContent: Separate expert behavior from novice (rules) and proficient (maxims), then remember the safety alert.
questions.hintStrategy: For each behavior, ask which Benner stage it belongs to; also eliminate anything that drops a safety practice.
